title: The Monarchy's Role in Keeping the Constitution on the Rails
label: 16 September 2026 · The King's private secretary
summary: The Constitution Committee questioned Lord Young of Old Windsor, former principal private secretary to the sovereign, about how the monarchy works in practice. He described the weekly private meetings between the monarch and the Prime Minister, the monarch's rights to be consulted, encourage and warn, and the rare reserve powers. He argued that confidentiality is essential, that the system relies on good faith and trust, and that while no system is perfect, he cannot see a better one; he suggested updating the Cabinet Manual.

speakers.label: Lord Young of Old Windsor
speakers.name: Lord Young of Old Windsor
speakers.role: Former Principal Private Secretary, The Royal Household

chapters.title: The weekly audience: where the relationship lives
chapters.takeaway: The core of the monarch's constitutional role is the private weekly meeting with the Prime Minister, where advice can be given freely because it stays confidential.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, Lord Young. You worked at the palace for a long time. How would you describe the monarch's role in everyday government today?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: I should declare I'm occasionally a paid consultant to the Royal Household. I worked for the late Queen for nearly 20 years and saw six Prime Ministers appointed—seven if you count Tony Blair's reappointment. The core of the relationship is the weekly audience with the PM. It was almost always at Buckingham Palace on a Wednesday after PMQs, usually 6.15 pm.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: I'd greet the PM, spend five or ten minutes alone, then they'd see the Queen for an hour. Meanwhile I'd spend the most useful constitutional hour of the week with the PM's principal private secretary—two sides of the golden triangle. My number one duty was to make sure there was never a gap between Head of State and Head of Government.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: The PM would come in walking a bit taller afterwards—who wouldn't want an hour a week with someone who won't put anything on X, won't gossip, won't write memoirs, and won't pursue a political view?

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The privacy of that meeting is crucial.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Absolutely. There's a tension between modern demands for openness and the need for privacy. But if we're to have this system, privacy is essential. I dealt with Freedom of Information requests even though the Royal Household isn't officially subject to the Act. The principle is that policy formulation—the discussions—is protected, not just the final policy. Otherwise people can't speak candidly.

chapters.title: When the monarch might push back
chapters.takeaway: The monarch has reserve powers for extreme situations, like picking a Prime Minister when it's unclear, but in practice the fear of them being used is a restraint.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: That weekly hour is significant. But could the monarch ever act as a restraint beyond that hour?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes. Our constitution isn't written down in one document; it's evolved through common law. The sovereign has the right to be consulted, encourage and warn. But the PM can say, 'Thank you, I've taken your counsel but I'm choosing to do something different.' That's the compact. However, there are reserve powers. For example, appointing a Prime Minister: usually on the outgoing PM's advice, but if it's not obvious who should be PM, the sovereign might take broader counsel. The private secretary would sound out the Cabinet Secretary and political leaders. Another example: if a government loses a no-confidence vote and the PM asks for a general election, the sovereign could theoretically decline. But if things work well, it should never get to that. The fear of the sovereign saying no is itself a restraint.

chapters.title: Opacity, good faith, and a Covid near-miss
chapters.takeaway: The unwritten nature of these powers allows flexibility; a real example from Covid showed how good faith and cooperation can handle a crisis.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: You said 'if things are working well'. But things might not always work well. Is it actually helpful that these reserve powers are a bit opaque and can develop in response to new situations?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes. The alternative would be a written constitution, but even then you can't spell out every eventuality. I have Boris Johnson's permission to mention an example. During Covid, when he was taken to hospital, there was a moment when it looked like he might need a ventilator. I got a call—I was at a bus shelter in the rain—saying the PM might not survive. We had no Deputy PM. The constitutional books didn't cover it.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: We worked out that the Cabinet Secretary would summon the Cabinet and not let them leave until they'd decided who to recommend as PM, possibly for a temporary period. Through the usual channels, someone was even getting hold of Jeremy Corbyn's office, which signalled it would sign up to the plan. It never happened, but it showed how everyone coming together worked. That relies on senior advisers having a rapport built up over time, caring about this niche topic, and not being partisan.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: What if a government loses a no-confidence vote but refuses to resign, and there's no alternative figure who can command a majority? What happens then?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It depends on the personalities and political mood. In a system that had broken down that badly, the sovereign might want to exercise greater power. Whether it would go as far as dismissing a Prime Minister—a Gough Whitlam scenario—would depend on events, but the reserve power exists. The fear of that happening has been a restrainer on government behaviour.

chapters.title: Trust, transparency and the 'head of nation' role
chapters.takeaway: The monarchy builds trust not through transparency but through long-term, non-partisan service as head of nation, which politicians can't do.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: You've described the weekly audience. But today the public demands transparency. How do you encourage trust in the establishment when it's so dependent on confidentiality?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It's a paradox: how can you have trust if you don't know what's going on? The advantage of our monarchy is that it's about the long term—the next year, five years, ten years—not tomorrow's headlines. It's about convening groups, recognising service, and representing the UK. Over time, that builds a feeling that the King or Queen is acting in the national interest, not partially. That's how you square the circle.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: So it's about visibility.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, certainly.

chapters.title: The King's past causes and the transition
chapters.takeaway: The King's previous campaigning on issues like climate change hasn't led to an interventionist monarch, and the transition was smooth.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Burry Port
turns.text: The King spent decades championing causes like climate change and architecture. How is that managed now that he must be neutral?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It's long been accepted that as heir you can pursue interests, but when you take the top job, those are put aside. The then Prince of Wales made that clear. Remember the drumbeat: 'He'll be an interventionist King, he'll reject bits of legislation.' None of that has happened. The transition was as smooth as could be hoped.

chapters.title: Could the monarchy stop a press crackdown?
chapters.takeaway: If a democratically elected government with a majority passed a law censoring the press, it would be very hard for the monarch or courts to overturn it.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: Supposing a government introduced censorship of the press and wanted to close down newspapers and broadcasters. What's the monarchy's role? Some call it the ultimate backstop, others say it's a broken reed.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It would depend on factors. Was this a manifesto commitment? Did it pass both Houses? If a democratically elected government with a majority pursued a manifesto commitment and it became law, it would be very difficult for a sovereign, or indeed the courts, to overturn that.

chapters.title: Guardians of the constitution
chapters.takeaway: The principal private secretary is a guardian of the constitution, though the role hasn't changed much since the 1950s.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: Who guards the constitution? Is the private secretary to the monarch a guardian?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, among many others. I see that as part of the role.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: Has that changed over time?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: No. I've spoken to many predecessors, and the principles are remarkably consistent back to the 1950s and 1960s.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Your predecessor Sir Alan Lascelles wrote an anonymous letter to The Times in 1950 setting out constitutional principles. Is that not evidence of a guardianship role?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes. Part of the role is to work out what's on the other side of the mountain—to get ahead of potential constitutional difficulties. Though I'm not sure an anonymous letter to The Times would work today; it'd become a headline. Better to make someone else think it was their idea.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Should the public better understand prerogative powers—the powers the monarch exercises on ministerial advice?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Both things can be true. It would do the country good to have greater understanding of our unique constitution at an earlier age. We don't really teach it in mainstream schooling.

chapters.title: Conventions, crises, and the Cabinet Manual
chapters.takeaway: Conventions evolve and are usually self-enforcing; Lord Young sees no better system but would like the Cabinet Manual updated.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You mentioned a PM not resigning after losing a confidence vote. Are conventions too lax? Is there a weakness?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Conventions evolve. In that scenario, a PM who lost confidence and refused to go would probably have no Cabinet left. The whole thing would crumble. It's hard to see them lasting long.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: I should declare I'm married to the Attorney-General. You mentioned Gough Whitlam. In 1975, the Governor-General dismissed him. Could that happen here? Jeremy Corbyn ignored a massive no-confidence vote in his leadership. That worries me.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Just because good practice has held doesn't mean it always will. The sovereign is the arbiter of last resort. But the current Governor-General of Australia said last year she couldn't see any Governor-General acting that way today, because the right to be consulted, encourage and warn is for the proper functioning of government, not for political judgments. I struggle to envisage a PM acting against convention but still supported by a working Cabinet. In the Whitlam case, the whole government had ground to a halt—people were worried about getting paid.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: So you're saying the safeguards are sufficient?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: I don't want to sound complacent. No system is perfect. But having seen it close up, I can't see a better one. That doesn't mean we shouldn't be vigilant. I'd like to see the Cabinet Manual updated—it's stuck in 2011. I'd also like every new PM to have the chance to review how it works. That would give me more comfort.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: In the face of a determined government that fully controls Parliament, are there any constitutional safeguards that could withstand them?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: If it's a democratically elected government pursuing a manifesto commitment, with a majority in the Commons, and it passes the Lords, it's very difficult to argue against. It's harder if more voters voted for another party but the constituency system produced a different result. Ultimately, this is a parliamentary democracy. If a democratically elected Parliament pursues its manifesto, it's hard to judge that as constitutionally improper.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: Is that a no?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It is what I answered.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Lord Young. That concludes this public session. We'll pause briefly before the next session with Lord Case.
